title: Pro Habits
description: Explore, plan, code, commit; verify everything; course-correct early and rewind without fear.

theory.title: Four phases, in order
theory.body:
Letting Claude jump straight to code can solve the wrong problem. Split the work:

**Explore**: Claude reads the relevant files and answers questions, no edits yet. **Plan mode** keeps it read-only. Turn it on by pressing `Shift+Tab` (cycles the permission modes) until the status bar shows plan mode on, or start with `claude --permission-mode plan`.

**Plan**: ask for a detailed implementation plan and fix it before any code exists.

**Code**: switch out of plan mode and implement, then **verify** with tests or checks.

**Commit**: commit with a descriptive message and open a PR.

Skip the plan for tiny changes: if you could describe the diff in one sentence, just ask.
theory.code:
$ claude --permission-mode plan      # or press Shift+Tab mid-session
> read @src/auth and explain how login works. don't change anything yet
> I want to add Google OAuth. what files change? create a plan
> implement the plan, write tests for the callback, run them and fix failures
> commit with a descriptive message and open a PR

theory.title: Give Claude a way to check itself
theory.body:
Claude stops when the work *looks* done. Give it something that returns pass or fail and it can iterate on its own:

**Tests**: behavior matches the spec. **Build** exit code: the project still compiles. **Linter**: style and suspicious patterns. **Type checker**: type mismatches. **Screenshot** vs a design mock: the UI matches.

So instead of "be careful", give concrete example cases and say "run the tests after implementing".

Work in **small, verifiable steps**: each one gets checked (and ideally committed) before the next. Kip never climbs to a new shell without testing the fit.

exercises.prompt: During the Explore phase, what should you tell Claude?
options: Implement the feature as fast as possible
Read the relevant files and explain them, but don't write any code yet
exercises.explanation: Exploring without edits means Claude understands the code before it changes anything, which is exactly what plan mode enforces.

exercises.prompt: When is it fine to skip the planning step?
options: When the change touches many files
When the change is small and clear, like fixing a typo or renaming a variable
When you're unfamiliar with the code
exercises.explanation: Planning costs time, so it only pays off when the change is big or unclear; a one-sentence diff can just be asked for.

exercises.prompt: Which gives Claude the strongest way to verify a new validateEmail function?
options: Asking it to be extra careful
Example cases plus 'run the tests after implementing'
exercises.explanation: Runnable test cases turn 'looks done' into a real pass/fail signal, which 'be careful' or a bigger model can't provide.

exercises.prompt: Match each check to what it verifies.
exercises.explanation: Each check returns a pass or fail Claude can read, which lets it fix its own mistakes instead of stopping when work merely looks done.

exercises.prompt: You want Claude to implement a dashboard design from a mock.
options: [Image #1] is the design. Implement it in src/Dashboard.tsx, take a screenshot of the result, compare it to the mock, list the differences, and fix them.
exercises.explanation: A screenshot compared to the mock gives Claude a concrete way to check its own work instead of guessing what 'better' means.

exercises.prompt: Two ways into read-only plan mode.
exercises.code:
$ claude --permission-mode ___
# or, mid-session, press ___ until the status bar shows plan mode on
exercises.explanation: Plan mode makes Claude read-only, and you can pick it at launch with the flag or switch into it mid-session with Shift+Tab.
exercises.hint: Start flag: --permission-mode <mode>. Mid-session shortcut: the key that cycles modes.

exercises.prompt: Put the pro workflow in order.
steps: Explore: have Claude read the relevant files, no code yet
Plan: ask for a detailed implementation plan
Code: implement the plan in small steps
Verify: run the tests, linter and type check
Commit: commit with a descriptive message
exercises.explanation: Understanding and planning before coding avoids solving the wrong problem, and verifying before committing keeps broken code out of history.

exercises.scenario: You need rate limiting on the login endpoint, and you're new to this codebase. Write a first prompt that explores and plans instead of jumping straight to code.
exercises.sample: Context: I'm new to this codebase and need rate limiting on login. Read @src/routes/auth.ts and @src/middleware/ and explain how requests reach the login handler and whether we already have rate-limiting utilities. Constraint: don't write code yet. Goal: propose a plan to rate limit login to 5 attempts per minute per IP, listing the files to change and the tests you'll add. Done when I have the explanation plus a step-by-step plan I can approve.
exercises.explanation: A strong first prompt explores, forbids edits for now, and asks for a plan that says how the result will be verified, so you can fix the approach before any code exists.

theory.title: Steer early, steer often
theory.body:
Tight feedback loops beat perfect first prompts. Kip's controls:

`Esc`: **interrupt** (stop) Claude mid-turn. Context is kept, so you can redirect.

`Esc` `Esc` (press twice with an empty input) or `/rewind`: open the **rewind** menu.

**"Undo that"**: ask Claude to revert its changes.

`/clear`: reset context between unrelated tasks.

Corrected Claude more than twice on the same thing? The context is full of failed attempts. `/clear` and start fresh with a sharper prompt that uses what you learned. A good correction says what to avoid, where to work, and how success is checked.
theory.code:
Esc       -> interrupt Claude mid-turn
Esc Esc   -> open the rewind menu (same as /rewind)
/clear    -> reset context between unrelated tasks

theory.title: Checkpoints and /rewind
theory.body:
Every prompt that starts a turn creates a **checkpoint**, a saved point you can go back to. In the rewind menu, pick a prompt and choose: **Restore code and conversation** (revert both), **Restore conversation** (rewind the chat, keep current code), **Restore code** (revert files, keep the chat), or **Summarize from here** (compress later messages into a summary).

Checkpoints track edits made by Claude's **file editing tools** only. Files changed by Bash commands like `rm` or `mv` aren't captured, so checkpoints don't replace **git**.

That's also why pros work in **small, verifiable steps**: mistakes surface early, and each step can be checked and committed before the next.

exercises.prompt: Claude is heading the wrong way mid-turn. Which key stops it while keeping the context?
exercises.explanation: Esc stops Claude immediately but keeps the conversation, so you can redirect without losing what it already learned.

exercises.prompt: Claude ran `rm old-config.json` through Bash. Can /rewind bring the file back?
options: No: checkpoints only track Claude's file-editing tools, so use git
Only if you press Esc three times
exercises.explanation: Checkpoints only see edits made by Claude's file tools, so Bash side effects like rm need git as the safety net.

exercises.prompt: You've corrected Claude twice on the same bug and it's still wrong. Best next move?
options: Keep correcting in the same session
/clear, then start fresh with a more specific prompt that uses what you learned
exercises.explanation: A long session full of failed attempts keeps steering Claude wrong, so a clean session with a sharper prompt usually works better.

exercises.prompt: Why work in small, verifiable steps?
options: Mistakes surface early, and each step can be checked and committed before the next
Claude can't edit more than one file per prompt
exercises.explanation: Small steps make each change easy to verify and easy to roll back, so a mistake costs one step instead of the whole task.

exercises.prompt: Match each rewind option to what it does.
exercises.explanation: Rewind lets you choose what to roll back, because sometimes the code was fine and only the conversation went wrong, or vice versa.

exercises.prompt: Claude started editing the database schema when you only wanted an API fix.
options: Stop: don't touch the database schema. Keep the change inside src/api/orders.ts and make the existing tests in tests/orders.test.ts pass.
exercises.explanation: A good correction says what to avoid, where to work, and how success is checked, so Claude doesn't have to guess again.

exercises.code:
Esc       -> ___ Claude mid-turn
Esc Esc   -> open the ___ menu
/___      -> reset context between tasks
exercises.explanation: Each control fixes a different problem: Esc stops a wrong turn, rewind undoes it, and /clear removes stale context.
exercises.hint: One key stops Claude, pressing it twice goes back in time, and a slash command wipes the slate.

exercises.prompt: Recover from a turn that went sideways.
steps: Press Esc to stop Claude mid-turn
Press Esc twice on an empty input to open the rewind menu
Select the prompt where things went wrong
Edit the restored prompt with clearer instructions and resend
exercises.explanation: Rewinding puts the original prompt back in the input, so you can sharpen it and retry from a clean state instead of piling on corrections.

exercises.prompt: Type the slash command that opens the rewind menu.
exercises.explanation: `/rewind` does the same as a double Esc, opening the checkpoints so you can restore code, conversation or both.

exercises.prompt: You finished one task and are starting an unrelated one. Type the slash command that resets the context.
exercises.explanation: Old context from an unrelated task distracts Claude and fills its memory, so `/clear` gives the new task a clean start.

mission.title: Run the Full Loop
mission.intro: Final boss: take one small, real task from question to commit like a pro.
checklist: Explore: in plan mode (Shift+Tab), ask Claude to read the relevant files and explain them
Plan: ask for a step-by-step plan that says how the change will be verified, then approve it
Code: have Claude implement it and run the tests (or linter/type check) until they pass
Practice a rewind: press Esc twice (or run /rewind) and restore an earlier checkpoint on one step
Commit: ask Claude to review the diff and commit with a descriptive message
mission.explanation: Explore, plan, verify, rewind and commit together are the habits that make Claude reliable on real work.

cheatsheet.description: Understand and plan before editing; verify, then commit.
Cycle permission modes, including read-only plan mode.
Start a session in plan mode.
Stop Claude mid-action; context is kept.
On an empty input, open the rewind menu.
Restore code and/or conversation to a checkpoint.
Track Claude's file edits per prompt; not Bash changes. Not a git replacement.
Tests, builds, linters, screenshots: a pass/fail Claude can check.
Corrected twice and still wrong? /clear and write a sharper prompt.
